newsitem.title: JAPAN: Metal markets calm after Deng's death, eye policies.
newsitem.headline: Metal markets calm after Deng's death, eye policies.

text.p: The world's metal markets, like other financial and commodity markets, reacted calmly on Thursday to the death of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, traders and analysts said.

They noted, however, that the reforms he set in place during his 18-year reign helped transform China into a major power in the marketplace, and any economic policy changes by Deng's successors that stunted the country's spectacular economic growth would dampen metals demand worldwide.
"If they turn to a tighter-money policy, domestic demand for copper and zinc will decline," said one veteran Japanese industry analyst.

Although he saw little reason to expect such a policy shift anytime soon, any sizable drop in demand in China, the world's largest importer of refined copper and exporter of refined zinc, would reverberate throughout world markets.

China's influence on world metal markets was apparent just hours before Deng's death on Wednesday, when rumours that China was replenishing its strategic reserves helped propel prices on the London Metal Exchange to their highest levels in more than eight months.

Several analysts have raised their copper price forecasts in recent weeks, due in large part to expectations that strong demand from China will help absorb a surge in global mine production over the next several years. China's imports rose nearly one-third last year to more than 700,000 tonnes.
A Macquarie Equities analyst estimated earlier this month that China could achieve sustained annual copper consumption growth of 10 to 15 percent.
China is also a leading world producer of many metals, including zinc, lead, tin and minor metals such as tungsten and antimony.
The Japanese analyst said any cut in China's domestic demand for zinc, for example, could lead to a rise in exports that would depress world prices.
At present, however, metals traders and analysts see no reason to expect Deng's death to affect the markets.
Indeed, London Metal Exchange prices barely budged when his death was announced during after-hours trade.
"Deng's death was not a surprise," said a senior metal trader with Tong Yang Global Corp in South Korea.

A copper trader at a big Japanese trade house said: "I don't see much impact from his death. Although it's still uncertain what policies China will pursue, metal demand in that country will be basically little changed."
Nor was Deng's death expected to have any immediate effect on Japanese investments in China's metals sector.

A spokesman for Sumitomo Metal Mining Co, which has a 20 percent stake in the 100,000-tonne-per-year Jinlong copper smelter project in China's Anhui Province, said the plant was still on track for start-up within the next few weeks.
